newsitem.title: USA: Northeast shareholders seen generating sparks.
newsitem.headline: Northeast shareholders seen generating sparks.

text.p: Northeast Utilities will likely generate some high-voltage sparks when it is confronted by frustrated shareholders at its annual meeting on Tuesday, analysts said Monday.

The utility, plagued by continuing shutdowns of its Millstone nuclear plants in Connecticut and a hostile deregulation environment in New Hampshire, must somehow assure shareholders that things are on an even keel.
"It's a horrible situation," said Jon Raleigh, managing director at Oppenheimer & Co in New York.
Northeast shares were down 0-1/8 at 9 at 1522 EDT.

"I wouldn't want to speculate on how bad it's going to be, but I think it would be safe to say that there will be shareholders who are less than pleased with the financial performance over the past year," Northeast spokeswoman Myra Humphries told Reuters.
Yet analysts said the meeting, scheduled for 1030 EDT in Agawam, Mass., promises to be more upbeat than last year's affair, because the nuclear wounds have had more time to heal.
"Now we're in the rebuilding period," Raleigh said. "As long as they're making progress and moving forward, that's what the shareholder today is looking for."

One of the main orders of business should be to convince investors that the 1,150 megawatt Millstone 3 plant will be ready for restart by the end of September, pending approval by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC), analysts said.
"From a shareholder point of view, they'll be interested in restart dates and how reliable they are," said Dan Scotto, analyst at Bear, Stearns & Co.
"The other big issue will obviously be management changes and the third will be, 'when are you going to reinstate my dividend?'
"The whole nuclear thing is really just dominating the landscape," Scotto said.
Northeast's three Millstone plants in Waterford, Conn., with a total capacity of almost 2,700 MW, have been closed for safety reasons since March 1996.
The utility has projected that its nuclear outage-related costs will reach $990 million by the end of 1998.
Northeast has said it intends to have Millstone 3 ready for restart in September, 870-MW unit 2 in November and 660-MW unit 1 sometime in early 1998, pending NRC approval.
Northeast's future hinges to some extent on its ability to get Millstone 3 back on line eventually, analysts said.

"One of the biggest factors affecting financial recovery, or reinstatement of the common dividend, is when they get the Millstone units -- all three of them -- but at the minimum one of them, Millstone 3, back on line," Scotto said.
"Because that's going to basically signal that the management has a firm handle on the nuclear problems and that they are making material progress toward turning them around."
He said the restart of Millstone 3 would be "the only concrete evidence or proof that things are going well, beyond rhetoric."
Northeast is also expected to give an update on its search for a new chief executive after Bernard Fox announced in February that he will retire in July.
Jittery shareholders will also need reassurance over the deregulation scenario in New Hampshire, where the utility has large exposure.

"In New Hampshire, there was a very punitive commission proposal put forth in February, which called for rate reductions and lack of stranded asset recovery," Raleigh said. Northeast is fighting a court battle over the decision and also trying to work out an agreement with the state.
But Scotto said shareholders could be in a forgiving mood, since Northeast actually hung onto its quarterly divided "several quarters" longer than it might have in the face of the nuclear crisis.
The utility on March 25 eliminated its 25 cent dividend.
